title: Swing-through: from behind, through the bird
summary: How swing-through works step by step, why you see little or no gap, and which targets it often suits.

body.html: In swing-through the muzzles start behind the target and overtake it. Coaches sum it up as “butt, belly, beak, bang”: tail, body, front, fire. Step by step, it looks like this:
The muzzles come from behind and fire as they pass the front of the target; the freeze-frame shows that the actual lead is bigger than it looked.
body.heading: Watch how the lead works

html: Start: the muzzles join the target’s line behind it, on its tail.
Overtaking: the gun moves faster than the target, along its line, through its body.
Shot: the trigger is pulled as the muzzles pass the front of the target, just ahead of it.
The swing continues after the shot.

body.html: There is a short delay between deciding to fire and the shot leaving the barrels. Because the gun is moving faster than the target, in that moment the barrels travel further ahead on their own. So you pull the trigger when you see little or no gap, and the gun’s speed adds the rest. The real lead at the shot is bigger than what you saw.

Strengths: it is natural and fast, and good for beginners. It suits close fast targets, driven targets (coming towards you and passing over your head), overheads from behind, and erratic or surprise targets.
Weaknesses: the window for the trigger is very short. On long crossers the shooter can run out of time, lose the line or overshoot. Slowing down as the muzzles reach the target gives a miss behind.

Coaches do not all use the same names for the lead methods. A name taken from a coaching school or an association can mean swing-through for one coach and pull-away for another. If a coach names a method that way, ask which one they mean.

notes.html: In British English you may hear “bum” instead of “butt”. It means the tail of the target, so translate it with a neutral word.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Come from behind, through the bird, and shoot as you see daylight.
phrases.meaning: Start behind the target, swing through it and fire as a gap appears in front.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Memory aid: tail, body, front of the target, then fire.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: You slowed down as you got to it.
phrases.meaning: The gun lost speed when it reached the target, so the shot went behind.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Brush it out and keep going.
phrases.meaning: Swing through the target as if wiping it out of the sky, without stopping.

key_points.html: Muzzles start behind, on the target's line.
Gun faster than the target: tail, body, front, bang.
Trigger as the muzzles pass the front; the actual lead is bigger than the lead seen.
Good for close, fast, driven and surprise targets; harder on long crossers.
A method named after a school can mean different methods: ask which one is meant.

quiz.q: Where do the muzzles start in swing-through?

options.text: At a fixed point at the break point
Behind the target, on its line

quiz.explain: Swing-through starts behind and overtakes the target; starting in front is maintained lead, a fixed point is ambush.

quiz.q: Why does a swing-through shooter see little or no lead?

options.text: The gun's speed creates the lead
The rules forbid a visible gap

quiz.explain: The gun moves faster than the target, so between deciding and firing it travels ahead by itself.

quiz.q: A coach says “bum, belly, beak, bang”. What does “bum” mean here?
quiz.explain: It means the tail of the target. A neutral word for “tail” keeps both the meaning and the rhythm of the memory aid.
